overview.text: Reverse osmosis (RO) is a membrane-based process that uses pressure to separate water from dissolved salts and other contaminants. A semipermeable membrane lets water pass more readily than many dissolved substances: the water that crosses is called permeate, while the remaining, more concentrated liquid is called concentrate or brine. By applying pressure to the salty feed water, RO drives water across the membrane while retaining much of its salt. This makes RO useful for desalination—removing salt from seawater or brackish water—and for treating drinking water. Its trade-offs include energy use and a concentrated reject stream that must be managed; pretreatment may also be needed to prevent membrane fouling.

key_facts.text: The process is pressure-driven: pumps pressurize feed water so water crosses a semipermeable membrane while salts are retained in concentrated brine.
Water passing through the membrane is called permeate or product water; the stream that does not pass through is called concentrate or reject.
RO is used to remove salts from seawater and brackish water, and can also remove a range of other dissolved contaminants.
The concentrate contains salts and removed contaminants, so it needs appropriate discharge or disposal.
High operating pressures can use significant energy, and pretreatment is often needed to help prevent membrane fouling or plugging.
